title: Sable and the Songbook
premise: Isandro Galloway, widowed father and owner of Bellwether Books, is coerced by the town library into an anonymous pen-pal program meant to boost festival attendance. His assigned correspondent turns out to be Marguerite Voss, the developer whose family firm is buying up Main Street—including, potentially, his bookshop. Through letters they fall for the stranger while clashing in person, each unaware of the other's identity until a stolen songbook of Marguerite's late mother's compositions surfaces in Isandro's rare-books crate. When the truth detonates at the Harvest Festival, Isandro must choose between the safe, contained heart he's built and the whole, risky one Marguerite's letters taught him to want; she must choose between her family's legacy and the town she's come to love. They end together, having saved the bookshop and published the songbook, choosing truth over every easier lie.
about_author: Sable Almeida is a former small-town librarian who now writes romance from a converted ferry cabin on the coast, where she keeps an embarrassing collection of secondhand songbooks. She believes every love story is really a story about what people are willing to be honest about, and when.

chapters.title: The Heart Is a Muscle
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Morning routine in Bellwether Books with his daughter Juniper establishes his philosophy: feelings can be trained, contained, shelved. The library's Ms. Okafor cornered him into the anonymous pen-pal program. Beat: guarded warmth, a man who has decided safety is the same as happiness.

chapters.title: Marguerite Arrives in Good Shoes
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She steps off the bus into Hollow Creek to assess the Voss Group's acquisition of Main Street, armed with a demolition schedule and her mother's unfinished songbook she can't bring herself to open. Beat: competence as armor; the town is a project, not a place.

chapters.title: Letters, First Ink
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating. Both receive their first anonymous letters; Isandro writes dry and precise, Marguerite writes sharp and funny. In person, they collide over a parking spot and despise each other instantly. Beat: dramatic irony planted—the reader sees what they can't.

chapters.title: The Enemy Across the Counter
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Marguerite tours the bookshop with a clipboard, and he gives her the coldest customer service of his life while Juniper charms her. That night his pen pal makes him laugh for the first time since his wife died. Beat: the split self begins—hostile by day, tender by night.

chapters.title: What the Voss Group Wants
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She presents the redevelopment plan at a hostile town meeting; Isandro speaks against it, eloquent and furious. Alone, she writes her pen pal about feeling like an instrument of someone else's will. Beat: her loyalty to family cracks under the weight of the town's faces.

chapters.title: Juniper's Reading List
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Juniper, eight and perceptive, asks why the clipboard lady looked sad. Isandro notices Marguerite lingering at the poetry shelf. His letter exchange turns unexpectedly vulnerable—he admits he's afraid of wanting things. Beat: the containable heart develops a leak.

chapters.title: Rain, and an Almost
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Caught in a storm, she shelters in the bookshop; Isandro makes tea, and something almost happens before her phone rings—her father, summoning her. She leaves without goodbye. Beat: proximity and retreat; the letters that night are the most honest yet.

chapters.title: The Songbook in the Crate
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Sorting a rare-books estate purchase, he finds a handwritten songbook inscribed to 'My Margo, finish it for me.' He recognizes Marguerite's family name and realizes her mother wrote it. Beat: the first secret he chooses to keep, and it sits in his chest like a stone.

chapters.title: Loyalty, Invoiced
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her father arrives in town, charming and ruthless, and orders the bookshop's lease terminated early. Marguerite signs the paperwork with a numb hand, then writes her pen pal that she may be a bad person. Beat: power's corruption becomes personal, and she feels herself complicit.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He learns of the lease termination and confronts Marguerite; the fight is vicious because it is intimate. Juniper witnesses the tail end and asks if the lady is the enemy. Beat: Isandro doubles down on containment—no more wanting, no more risk.

chapters.title: The Letter That Names It
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her pen pal writes that he's falling for someone impossible, and she realizes she is too. She drafts a confession of who she is and what she's done, then can't send it. Beat: truth and loyalty at open war inside her; the unsent letter burns in her bag.

chapters.title: Festival Preparations
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The town prepares the Harvest Festival; Ms. Okafor announces the pen-pal reveal ceremony. Isandro and Marguerite are forced onto the same committee, trading civility that costs them both. Beat: the clock starts ticking toward the reveal both dread and crave.

chapters.title: What Juniper Found
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Juniper finds the songbook and asks him to play it; he does, badly, and weeps. He resolves to return it to Marguerite honestly—but then discovers her signature on his lease termination in the same stack of papers. Beat: grief and betrayal fuse; he pockets the songbook and his honesty.

chapters.title: The Wrong Kind of Brave
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She defies her father privately, delaying the demolition, and he threatens to reveal how she obtained the songbook's copyright—a legal fiction she signed. Beat: her father's power corrupts through her; she realizes loyalty to him has made her a liar twice over.

chapters.title: Almost Confessions
chapters.summary: Dual POV. On the festival's eve, Isandro and Marguerite nearly tell each other everything—twice. Each retreats into the letters instead, promising their anonymous stranger the truth they can't give each other. Beat: the dramatic irony reaches maximum pressure; the reader aches.

chapters.title: The Reveal
chapters.summary: Dual POV. At the festival's pen-pal ceremony, envelopes are opened publicly. Isandro reads his letter aloud—Marguerite's confession of who she is—and the town hears it before he processes it. She reads his, which names her as the person he's falling for. Beat: the climax's first detonation; public ruin.

chapters.title: Everything True and Unbearable
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He confronts Marguerite privately: the letters, the lease, the songbook he's been hiding. She learns he knew about the songbook and said nothing. Both accusations land. Beat: the midpoint's contained hearts shatter completely; both are right and both are wrong.

chapters.title: The Empty Shop
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She tears up the acquisition contract, resigns from the Voss Group, and her father disowns her by phone. She plays her mother's songbook—Isandro leaves it anonymously at her hotel—alone in the shuttered bookshop. Beat: identity rebuilt from the wreckage of inherited power.

chapters.title: What Juniper Knew All Along
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Juniper, who has been secretly writing her own letters to 'the clipboard lady,' stages a small intervention with Ms. Okafor's help. Isandro reads his daughter's letter and understands he taught her containment when he meant to teach her caution. Beat: the father learns from the child; the choice crystallizes.

chapters.title: The Whole Heart
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At the festival's final night, Isandro takes the stage, plays the songbook's unfinished last piece badly and completely, and tells the whole town the truth—every letter, every lie, every feeling. Beat: the climax's resolution; risk chosen over safety, publicly and irreversibly.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Answer
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She answers not with words but with the songbook's final page—her mother's last line completed in her own hand, delivered to the bookshop with a single sentence: 'The heart was never a muscle. It's a door.' Beat: forgiveness as a decision, not a feeling.

chapters.title: Bellwether, Reopened
chapters.summary: Dual POV, converging. Spring: the bookshop reopens with a music corner and the published songbook on the shelf; Juniper has two last names' worth of people fussing over her. Isandro and Marguerite write each other one final letter—handed over in person. Beat: identity, loyalty, and truth resolved into one chosen life.
